text: A federal court let officers press a man's own thumb to his phone. Then it added a line that undoes almost everything.
provenance: In 2024, a federal appeals court — the Ninth Circuit — looked at a case where officers took a man's phone and simply pressed his own thumb to the sensor to unlock it.

text: In 2024 the Ninth Circuit said pressing a thumb takes no thought at all. His body opened the door against him, and the Constitution had nothing to say about it.
provenance: The court said that did not violate the Fifth Amendment. Pressing a thumb, they reasoned, takes no thought at all. His body opened the door against him — and the Constitution had nothing to say about it.

text: But the court hinted the answer might have been different if the officers had made the man choose which finger to use.
provenance: The court hinted the answer might have been different if the officers had made the man choose which finger to use

text: Because choosing is a decision, and a decision happens in your mind. Same thumb. No protection if they press it. Maybe protected if you decide.
provenance: because choosing is a decision, and a decision happens in your mind
A thumb they press to the sensor: no protection. The very same thumb, if you are the one who decides to use it: maybe protected.

text: So what protects you is not the lock on the phone. It is whether the choice to open it was ever yours.
